Bremen
brem'en
n. (free Hanse city and archbishopric on the Weser; a Lutheran city that became Reformed over the Lord's Supper)
From Old Saxon Bremon, perhaps at the edge or brim; Latin Brema.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Bremen changed confession twice and both times over the Supper. It reformed as a Lutheran city in the 1520s, and then from 1547 its cathedral preacher Albert Hardenberg taught the Reformed doctrine of the sacrament; the quarrel ran for a decade, Hardenberg was expelled in 1561, and within a generation the city had followed him anyway, adopting a Reformed order and in 1595 the Bremen Consensus. The dictionary records Bremen because the city was willing to spend ten years on one question, having judged that how Christ is present to His people in the ordinance is not a detail. The Reformed answer is the one the dictionary holds: the bread and the cup are a true communion of the body and blood of Christ to the believer by faith, and not a sacrifice, and not a change of substance. “The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?” (1Co 10:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines communion as fellowship and intercourse, and the body of Christians who partake of the Lord's supper; a sacrament as, among the ancient Romans, an oath taken by soldiers to be true to their general.

expand to see more

COMMU'NION, n. Fellowship; intercourse between two persons or more; the body of Christians who partake of the Lord's supper.

SACRAMENT, n. Among the ancient Romans, an oath taken by soldiers to be true to their general.

BREAD, n. A mass of dough, made by moistening and kneading the flour or meal of some species of grain, and baked in an oven.

SUPPER, n. The evening meal. People who dine at noon call their evening meal supper.

Key Scripture

1Co 10:16 — "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?"

1Co 11:26 — "For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come."

Mat 26:26 — "And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body."

Joh 6:63 — "It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life."

Modern Corruption

A Hanse city that spent a decade on the Lord's Supper, expelled Hardenberg, and then followed him into the Reformed confession.

expand to see more

The corruptions of the Supper are live on every side. Rome teaches a change of substance and a propitiatory sacrifice offered by a priest; the Lutheran formula locates the body in, with and under the elements; and a wide modern evangelicalism has emptied the ordinance in the other direction, treating it as a bare remembrance in which nothing is received and little is risked. All three are named here as departures.

The principle to recover is that the ordinance is a true communion in which Christ is received spiritually by faith. Paul calls it exactly that: “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?” (1Co 10:16). It is also a proclamation bounded by time: “ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26). The institution is plain and was given with the Lord's own body still at the table: “Take, eat; this is my body” (Mat 26:26). And the manner of receiving is spiritual, on His own authority: “It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek koinonia (G2842), communion, having in common; Greek katangello (G2605), to proclaim.

Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, a having in common; 1 Corinthians 10:16.

Greek eulogia (G2129) — blessing, the cup of blessing; 1 Corinthians 10:16.

Greek katangello (G2605) — to announce, to proclaim openly; 1 Corinthians 11:26.

Greek eucharisteo (G2168) — to give thanks; compare Matthew 26:27.

Greek zoopoieo (G2227) — to make alive, to quicken; John 6:63.

Usage

"“is it not the communion of the body of Christ?” (1Co 10:16) — Hardenberg at the cathedral from 1547."

"“ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26) — expelled in 1561, and the city followed him."

"“It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63) — the Bremen Consensus of 1595."
